questions.stem: What is homeostasis?
options: Changing the internal environment to match the outside
Stopping all chemical reactions when conditions change
Maintaining a relatively constant internal environment
Keeping the external environment at a fixed temperature
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the maintenance of relatively constant internal conditions, such as temperature, water balance and blood glucose, so that cells work in optimum conditions. Conditions vary within a narrow range rather than staying exactly fixed.

questions.stem: Why can a body temperature well above the normal range be dangerous?
options: Enzymes work faster forever, so cells run out of space
Cells stop taking in water, so the blood volume rises
Nerve impulses travel backwards along the neurons
Enzymes may denature, so metabolic reactions fail
questions.explanation: Organisms survive best within tolerance limits. Above them, proteins such as enzymes can lose their shape and stop working, disrupting metabolism. Faster reactions cannot continue indefinitely, because the enzymes become denatured.

questions.stem: Which list gives factors for which humans have tolerance limits, as regulated by homeostasis?
options: Body temperature, water, blood glucose and blood carbon dioxide
Hair colour, height, eye colour and the number of fingers
Air pressure, day length, wind speed and the phase of the moon
The number of chromosomes, blood group and skin colour
questions.explanation: Body temperature, water availability, blood glucose level and carbon dioxide concentration in the blood and tissues all have tolerance limits and are regulated. Inherited traits such as blood group are not regulated by homeostasis.

questions.stem: In the stimulus-response model, what is the role of an effector?
options: To detect a change in the internal or external environment of the body
To carry impulses from the receptors to the central nervous system
To compare a change with the set point and decide on a response
To carry out a response, such as a muscle contracting or a gland secreting
questions.explanation: Effectors are muscles and glands that produce the response. Receptors detect the stimulus, sensory neurons carry the message, and the control centre, such as the hypothalamus, processes it.

questions.stem: What is the role of sensory receptors?
options: To break down neurotransmitters at the synapse after use
To detect changes in the internal or external environment
To release hormones into the blood in response to a change
To contract and move the body away from a harmful stimulus
questions.explanation: Receptors detect stimuli, such as temperature, pressure, light or chemical concentrations, and convert them into nerve impulses. Responding by contracting or secreting is the job of effectors.

questions.stem: Which statement describes negative feedback?
options: The response reduces or reverses the original stimulus
The response increases the size of the original stimulus
The response continues even after the stimulus is gone
The response happens only when no stimulus is present
questions.explanation: In negative feedback, the response counteracts the change that triggered it, returning the variable towards its normal level. For example, sweating cools the body, reducing the rise in temperature that caused it.

questions.stem: Blood glucose rises after a meal and insulin is released. As glucose falls back to normal, insulin release decreases. Why is this an example of negative feedback?
options: The meal itself is the response, and the insulin is the original stimulus
The fall in glucose caused by insulin reduces the stimulus for insulin release
The rise in insulin increases glucose further, so even more insulin is released
Insulin release continues at the same rate whatever the blood glucose level is
questions.explanation: The response (lower blood glucose) removes the stimulus (high blood glucose), so insulin secretion falls. This prevents glucose from overshooting too far below normal.

questions.stem: Which structures make up the central nervous system?
options: The brain and spinal cord
The nerves and sense organs
The spinal cord and nerves
The brain and endocrine glands
questions.explanation: The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) consists of the nerves that connect the CNS to receptors and effectors throughout the body.

questions.stem: Which comparison of neuron types is correct?
options: Sensory neurons carry impulses to the CNS; motor neurons carry impulses from the CNS
Motor neurons carry impulses to the CNS; sensory neurons carry impulses from the CNS
Interneurons carry impulses from receptors in the skin to muscles in the arm
Sensory and motor neurons are both found only within the brain and spinal cord
questions.explanation: Sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors to the CNS, interneurons connect neurons within the CNS, and motor neurons carry impulses from the CNS to effectors.

questions.stem: What is the correct sequence of a nerve pathway from receptor to effector?
options: Receptor, interneuron, sensory neuron, effector, motor neuron
Receptor, sensory neuron, interneuron, motor neuron, effector
Receptor, motor neuron, interneuron, sensory neuron, effector
Effector, sensory neuron, interneuron, motor neuron, receptor
questions.explanation: A stimulus is detected by a receptor, carried by a sensory neuron to the CNS, passed on by interneurons, and sent by a motor neuron to an effector, which responds.

questions.stem: How is an impulse passed from one neuron to the next at a synapse?
options: The electrical impulse jumps directly across the gap without any chemical signal
The two neurons fuse together briefly so the impulse can flow through the join
A hormone travels in the blood from one neuron to the other across the gap
A neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap and binds to receptors on the next neuron
questions.explanation: When an impulse reaches the axon terminal, vesicles release neurotransmitter, which diffuses across the synaptic gap and binds to specific receptors on the next neuron, triggering an impulse there.

questions.stem: Why do impulses travel in only one direction across a synapse?
options: Impulses can only travel towards the brain, so synapses always point towards the head
Neurotransmitter is released only by the axon terminal, and receptors are only on the next cell
Neurotransmitter is released by both neurons, but it can only diffuse from the larger cell
The synaptic gap is filled with a solid that lets molecules pass in only one direction
questions.explanation: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are found only in the presynaptic terminal, and the receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane, so the signal passes one way. Motor pathways carry impulses away from the brain.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the enzyme that breaks down the neurotransmitter acetylcholine at synapses with muscles. What effect would be expected?
options: Acetylcholine is never released, so muscles cannot contract at all
Impulses travel backwards from the muscles to the spinal cord
The muscle fibres take up acetylcholine as an energy source
Acetylcholine stays in the gap, so muscles keep being stimulated
questions.explanation: Normally an enzyme quickly breaks down acetylcholine so each signal is brief. If the enzyme is blocked, acetylcholine remains bound to receptors, causing continuous stimulation and uncontrolled muscle contraction.

questions.stem: What are the features of a reflex response?
options: Slow, hormonal and long-lasting
Rapid, learned and conscious
Rapid, automatic and involuntary
Slow, learned and voluntary
questions.explanation: A reflex is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not need conscious thought, such as pulling a hand away from a hot plate. It protects the body by minimising response time.

questions.stem: When a person touches a hot plate, their hand is withdrawn before they feel pain. Why?
options: The pain receptors are directly attached to the muscles of the arm
Hormones released by the skin reach the arm muscles before impulses reach the brain
The brain sends the impulse to the arm before receiving it from the hand
The reflex pathway passes through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain
questions.explanation: In a spinal reflex, the sensory neuron connects through an interneuron in the spinal cord directly to a motor neuron, so the muscle responds quickly. Impulses also travel up the cord to the brain, where pain is felt slightly later.

questions.stem: How do hormones reach their target cells?
options: They move through lymph nodes only
They travel in the blood
They travel along neurons
They diffuse through the air
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands secrete hormones into the blood, which carries them throughout the body. Only target cells with specific receptors for a hormone respond to it.

questions.stem: Hormones can be amino acid derivatives, peptides, proteins or steroids. Which hormone is a steroid?
options: Insulin
Adrenaline
Antidiuretic hormone
Testosterone
questions.explanation: Steroid hormones such as testosterone, oestrogen and cortisol are made from cholesterol. Insulin and ADH are peptides or proteins, and adrenaline is an amino acid derivative.

questions.stem: A hormone circulates in the blood past every cell in the body, but only liver and muscle cells respond to it. What is the best explanation?
options: Only those cells are close enough to the gland that releases the hormone
Only those cells have a nucleus, so only they can take up the hormone
Only those cells are connected to neurons that carry the hormone to them
Only those cells have receptors with a shape complementary to the hormone
questions.explanation: Target cells have specific receptor proteins that bind the hormone. Cells without the receptor are not affected, even though the hormone reaches them in the blood.

questions.stem: Which comparison of insulin and glucagon is correct?
options: Both raise blood glucose, but at different times
Both lower blood glucose by storing it as fat
Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it
Insulin raises blood glucose; glucagon lowers it
questions.explanation: Insulin, released when blood glucose is high, increases glucose uptake by cells and its conversion to glycogen. Glucagon, released when glucose is low, stimulates the liver to break down glycogen to glucose.

questions.stem: Several hours after a meal, blood glucose falls below normal. Which response restores it?
options: Insulin is released, and cells take up more glucose from the blood
ADH is released, and the kidneys reabsorb more glucose from urine
Thyroxine falls, and cells stop using glucose for respiration altogether
Glucagon is released, and the liver converts glycogen to glucose
questions.explanation: Cells in the islets of the pancreas detect low glucose and release glucagon. Glucagon causes liver cells to break down stored glycogen and release glucose into the blood.

questions.stem: How can diabetes mellitus result from a hormonal imbalance?
options: Too much insulin is made, so the blood glucose level stays far too high
Too much glucagon is stored in the liver, so no glucose enters the blood
Too little ADH is made, so glucose is lost from the body in sweat
Too little insulin is made, or cells respond poorly to it, so glucose stays high
questions.explanation: In type 1 diabetes the pancreas produces little or no insulin; in type 2, cells respond poorly to insulin. Either way, glucose is not taken up from the blood effectively, so blood glucose stays high.

questions.stem: A person with type 1 diabetes injects insulin but then skips a meal and exercises. Why are they at risk of a dangerously low blood glucose level?
options: Insulin raises blood glucose, so exercise lowers it far more than in other people
Exercise destroys injected insulin, so the liver converts all glucose to glycogen
Skipping a meal increases insulin production by their own pancreas
Insulin keeps moving glucose into cells while exercise uses glucose and none is eaten
questions.explanation: The injected insulin continues to drive glucose into cells, while exercising muscles use more glucose and no food replaces it. Without the normal reduction in insulin, blood glucose can fall too low.

questions.stem: What is the role of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)?
options: It speeds up the heart rate during the fight or flight response
It stimulates the thyroid gland to produce and release thyroxine
It lowers blood glucose by increasing glucose uptake by muscle
It increases the reabsorption of water in the collecting ducts
questions.explanation: TSH is released by the pituitary gland and travels in the blood to the thyroid, stimulating it to produce thyroxine. This is an example of a hormonal response stimulated by another hormone.

questions.stem: What is the main effect of thyroxine on body cells?
options: It increases the metabolic rate, including the rate of respiration
It decreases the metabolic rate, so cells use less oxygen
It converts glycogen into glucose only in the liver cells
It makes the collecting ducts of the kidney permeable to water
questions.explanation: Thyroxine acts on most body cells, increasing their metabolic rate and therefore respiration and heat production. Glycogen breakdown is mainly controlled by glucagon and adrenaline.

questions.stem: A blood test shows high thyroxine and very low TSH. How does negative feedback explain this?
options: High thyroxine inhibits TSH release from the pituitary gland
Low TSH stimulates the thyroid to produce even more thyroxine
High thyroxine stimulates the pituitary gland to release more TSH
TSH and thyroxine are unrelated, so the result shows nothing
questions.explanation: Thyroxine feeds back to the hypothalamus and pituitary, reducing TSH release when thyroxine levels are high. Very low TSH alongside high thyroxine is the expected feedback response.

questions.stem: What is the effect of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) on the nephron?
options: It makes the collecting ducts less permeable to water, so more is lost
It causes glucose to be actively secreted into the urine by the tubule
It makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more is reabsorbed
It makes the glomerulus filter more water, so more urine is produced
questions.explanation: ADH increases the number of water channels (aquaporins) in the walls of the collecting ducts, so more water moves back into the blood by osmosis. The result is a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

questions.stem: After a long run on a hot day without drinking, a person's urine is dark and small in volume. Which sequence explains this?
options: Blood becomes dilute, more ADH is released, less water is reabsorbed
Blood becomes concentrated, more ADH is released, more water is reabsorbed
Blood becomes dilute, less ADH is released, more water is reabsorbed
Blood becomes concentrated, less ADH is released, less water is reabsorbed
questions.explanation: Water lost in sweat raises the solute concentration of the blood, which is detected in the hypothalamus. More ADH is released from the pituitary, so the kidneys reabsorb more water and produce concentrated urine.

questions.stem: Alcohol reduces the release of ADH. Which effect would be expected after drinking alcohol?
options: Glucose appearing in the urine because filtration stops
A larger volume of dilute urine and a risk of dehydration
A smaller volume of concentrated urine and a rise in blood volume
No change in urine, because ADH acts only on sweat glands
questions.explanation: With less ADH, the collecting ducts are less permeable to water, so less water is reabsorbed and more dilute urine is produced. Losing extra water can cause dehydration.

questions.stem: How does the release of ADH affect blood pressure?
options: More water is reabsorbed, raising blood volume and so blood pressure
Less water is reabsorbed, raising blood volume and so blood pressure
More water is lost in urine, lowering blood volume and raising pressure
ADH has no effect on blood volume or blood pressure at all
questions.explanation: Osmoregulation, blood volume and blood pressure are linked. When ADH increases water reabsorption, more water stays in the blood, raising blood volume and therefore blood pressure.

questions.stem: Which effects does adrenaline have in the fight or flight response?
options: Narrower airways, and less blood flowing to skeletal muscles
Faster heart rate and breathing, and more glucose released into the blood
Slower heart rate and breathing, and more glucose stored as glycogen
More blood to the gut, and a lower metabolic rate in the muscles
questions.explanation: Adrenaline prepares the body for action: it increases heart rate and breathing rate, widens airways, diverts blood to muscles and raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown.

questions.stem: During a sudden fright, nerve impulses travel from the brain to the adrenal glands, which release adrenaline. What does this show?
options: The endocrine system works only when the nervous system is inactive
Hormones can only ever be stimulated by other hormones in the blood
A hormonal response can be stimulated by the nervous system
Adrenaline is a neurotransmitter carried only along motor neurons
questions.explanation: Hormone release can be triggered by nerve impulses, as with adrenaline from the adrenal glands, or by other hormones, as with thyroxine release triggered by TSH.

questions.stem: Which comparison of nervous and endocrine control is correct?
options: Nervous messages travel in the blood; endocrine messages travel along neurons
Nervous responses affect the whole body; endocrine responses affect one muscle only
Nervous responses are fast and short-lived; endocrine responses are slower and longer-lasting
Nervous responses are slow and long-lasting; endocrine responses are fast and short-lived
questions.explanation: Nerve impulses travel rapidly along neurons to specific effectors, giving fast, brief responses. Hormones travel in the blood, take longer to act, often affect several targets and have longer-lasting effects.

questions.stem: On a cold day, which responses help to maintain body temperature?
options: Vasoconstriction in the skin and shivering
Vasodilation in the skin and sweating
Sweating and a lower metabolic rate
Vasodilation in the skin and less thyroxine
questions.explanation: Narrowing skin blood vessels (vasoconstriction) reduces heat loss, and shivering generates heat by muscle contraction. Thyroxine and adrenaline can also raise metabolic rate. Sweating and vasodilation are responses to heat.

questions.stem: Body temperature regulation involves both systems. Which pairing correctly shows a nervous and a hormonal part of the response to cold?
options: Nervous: thyroxine causes shivering; hormonal: impulses raise metabolic rate
Nervous: ADH reduces sweating; hormonal: insulin causes vasoconstriction
Nervous: glucagon dilates vessels; hormonal: impulses stimulate sweat glands
Nervous: impulses cause shivering; hormonal: more thyroxine raises metabolic rate
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus sends impulses to skeletal muscles (shivering) and skin arterioles (vasoconstriction), and stimulates hormonal pathways that increase thyroxine release, raising heat production by cells over a longer time.

questions.stem: During exercise, carbon dioxide in the blood rises and the pH of the fluid around the brain falls. What response follows?
options: The pancreas releases insulin, which converts the carbon dioxide into glycogen
The kidneys release ADH, which removes carbon dioxide from the blood as urine
Chemoreceptors in the brain detect the pH fall, and breathing rate and depth increase
Chemoreceptors in the brain detect the pH rise, and breathing rate and depth decrease
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, lowering pH. Chemoreceptors in the brain detect this and send impulses to the breathing muscles, increasing the rate and depth of breathing so more carbon dioxide is exhaled and pH returns to normal.

questions.stem: Which hormone and gland are correctly matched?
options: Thyroxine: the adrenal glands
Adrenaline: the thyroid gland
TSH: the islet cells of the pancreas
Insulin: the islet cells of the pancreas
questions.explanation: Insulin and glucagon come from the islet cells of the pancreas, thyroxine from the thyroid, adrenaline from the adrenal glands, and TSH and ADH are released from the pituitary gland.
